title: Red rice vs brown rice vs white rice: what’s the difference?
summary: How red, brown and white rice differ in milling and bran colour, plus cooking times, water ratios and how to store each kind.
body:
Red rice, brown rice and white rice can all come from the same kind of plant. What separates them is mostly two things: the colour of the bran layer, and how much of that bran the mill leaves on the grain.

## What a rice grain is made of

A harvested rice grain, called paddy, has four parts:

- **Husk** (or hull): the tough outer shell, which you can't eat. Every kind of rice has it removed.
- **Bran**: thin layers wrapped around the grain. In most rice it is light brown; in red rice it is reddish-brown.
- **Germ**: the small embryo at one end of the grain.
- **Endosperm**: the white, starchy inside, which makes up most of the grain.

## The three kinds, side by side

### White rice

White rice has been husked and then polished: rubbed until the bran and germ are worn away, leaving only the endosperm. It cooks quickly, tastes mild and keeps for a long time, because the oily bran is gone. Most rice sold around the world is white. Read more in [polished vs unpolished rice](/learn/polished-vs-unpolished-rice/).

### Brown rice

Brown rice is husked but not polished, so it keeps its bran and germ. "Brown" describes the colour of the bran, not a special variety. Almost any rice, including basmati and jasmine, can be sold as brown rice. It is chewier and nuttier than white rice and takes longer to cook.

### Red rice

Red rice is also husked and left with its bran, but it comes from varieties whose bran is red. The colour comes from pigments called anthocyanins in the bran layer. Red rice varieties are grown across India, from Kerala and the Konkan coast to the Himalayan foothills, and in many other rice-growing countries.

One catch: if red rice is polished, the red bran goes with it and the grain turns mostly white. So "red rice" is only red when it is unpolished or lightly polished. Check the pack, or look at the grains: unpolished red rice is red-brown all the way round.

## At a glance

- **Milling**: white is husked and polished; brown and red are husked only, or lightly polished.
- **Bran and germ**: gone in white; kept in brown and red.
- **Colour**: white; light brown; red to reddish-brown.
- **Texture**: soft, tender grains in white; chewier and nuttier in brown; chewy and earthy in red.
- **Keeping time**: longest for white; shorter for brown and red, because their bran contains oil.

## Cooking times and water ratios

These are starting points for the stovetop absorption method, by volume. A standard 240 ml cup holds about 180–200 g of uncooked rice. Grain size, age and variety all change the numbers, so check the pack and adjust.

- **White rice**: rinse, then 1 cup rice to 1½–2 cups water. Simmer covered for about 12–18 minutes.
- **Brown rice**: rinse and soak 30 minutes, then 1 cup rice to 2–2½ cups water. Simmer covered for about 35–45 minutes.
- **Red rice**: rinse and soak 30 minutes, then 1 cup rice to about 2¼ cups water. Simmer covered for about 30–40 minutes.

Let any rice rest, covered and off the heat, for 10 minutes before fluffing it with a fork. In a pressure cooker, soaked unpolished rice usually needs about 3–4 whistles on medium heat. For a full method and troubleshooting, see [how to cook unpolished rice](/learn/how-to-cook-unpolished-rice/).

## How to store each kind

- **White rice**: airtight, in a cool, dry cupboard. It keeps well for a long time.
- **Brown and red rice**: airtight, cool, dry and dark. The oil in the bran slowly goes stale with heat and time, so buy amounts you'll use within a few months and use it before the best-before date. In a hot, humid kitchen, keep it in the fridge.
- **Any rice**: a stale, sour or musty smell means it is past its best. Small insects such as rice weevils are a sign that a container wasn't airtight. Clean and dry it fully before refilling.

## Which one should you choose?

That comes down to taste and use. White rice is soft and quick. Brown and red rice are chewier and nuttier, hold their shape, and suit khichdi (a one-pot dish of rice and lentils), pulao and grain bowls.
